title: §1 Unrelated equalities make types interchangeable (fixsubst) and the eqrefute companion

reviews.summary: The mechanism is right. Tracing the baseline confirms that Typer.match's coercion path drops the substitutions from its own unification. That lets ?e := A.X be re-bound to D.X by reflexivity, and I found no other path that drops substitutions. What is wrong is the description of which programs are affected. With a single equality in scope, a type that appears in no equality can be proved equal to a side of that equality whenever the equality goal comes from a call-site requirement or a given's premise. The 'two equalities / both types on a side' pattern only shows up when a value is passed as an argument, because coerced() checks the outer pair with canDeriveCoercions before searching.

issues.title: Affected-program description is wrong: a single equality is enough, and the other type need not appear in any equality
issues.evidence: I ran all of these on the impl10 binary at the default depth, with flags off. c01: `fun g<T, U where T == U>() {}  fun f<V, W, D where V == W>() { g<D, V>() }` is accepted with 0 diagnostics. Its trace (trace-c01.txt) shows the same derivation: transitivity<D, %e, V>, then the given V~W coerced to (%e ~ V) assuming W~V, then reflexivity rebinds %e := D, and the result is g<D, V>(transitivity<D,D,V>(refl<D>)(coercion($g))). c04: single equality A.X == B.X, and `g<D.X, A.X>()` is accepted. c06: `fun f<V where V == S>() { g<Q, S>() }` is accepted, where Q is an unrelated concrete struct. c07: single equality, and `let y: A.X = h<D.X, A.X>(x)` with x: D.X is accepted, which is a real value cast. c03: single equality V == W plus a local `given <X where X == V> => X is P`, and `need<D>()` is accepted. fixsubst (cap 7) rejects all of them, and fixsubst,eqrefute rejects c01, c06 and c07 in under 60 ms.
issues.correction: Replace 'any type mentioned on a side of some equality ... once two equalities are in scope; types mentioned in no equality are still rejected' with the following. An equality goal L ~ R is wrongly proved whenever R is a side of some equality given whose other side is a different type. Reaching it takes a depth cap of at least 7. L can be any type, including one that appears in no equality, when the goal is an implicit requirement at a call site, a given's premise, or similar. When the goal comes from argument or annotation coercion (coerced()), its top-level canDeriveCoercions(root.type, goal) check also requires L to unify with a side of some equality given. Only then does a second equality become necessary. The repro header line 'with a single equality the program is correctly rejected' is true only for that coerced() path.

issues.title: Why two equalities are needed in the repros is an artifact of coerced()'s top-level pre-filter, not part of the cause
issues.evidence: Typer.swift coerced(): `if canDeriveCoercions(root.type, goal, in: scopeOfUse, where: .empty)` is applied to the closed pair (D.X, A.X) before resolution starts. Inside the bogus derivation, the only coercion that gets filtered is (B.X, A.X) (or (W, V)), and both of those are sides of the same given. v01 (single equality, argument passing) is rejected, but c04 (the same types, as a call-site requirement) is accepted.
issues.correction: State this explicitly. Otherwise readers will assume single-equality code is safe, and the generated assocneg workloads cover only the argument-passing entry point.

issues.title: The bogus derivation needs 7 resolution layers; at a depth cap of 6 or less the baseline rejects
issues.evidence: bug-assoc-eq-two-links.hylo baseline: HYLO_TC_MAXDEPTH=6 gives diagnostics 1 (summon.depthExhausted=1). At 7, 8 and 10 it gives diagnostics 0. The trace says 'resolve (A::P).X: 7 layers, 1 done'.
issues.correction: Say that the wrong acceptance depends on the depth cap being at least 7. This matters when experiments use small caps.

issues.title: Closed under type constructors: types mentioned in no equality but built from such types are also interchangeable
issues.evidence: v03: A.X == B.X and C.X == D.X; passing x: Box<D.X> to check<Box<A.X>> is accepted by the baseline (0 diagnostics). With fixsubst it is rejected (14 s). The match on Box<...> produces a part coercion (D.X, A.X).
issues.correction: Add 'and any type built from them by congruence (e.g. Box<D.X> vs Box<A.X>)'.

issues.title: Equalities do not have to involve associated types; with structured sides, the fixed configuration crashes instead of rejecting
issues.evidence: v02: `fun f<A,B,C,D where A == B, C == D>(x: D) { check<A>(x) }` is accepted by the baseline. With fixsubst alone it runs out of memory ('failed to allocate 402653240 bytes'). With fixsubst,eqrefute it is rejected in 14 ms. v04: `A == Box<B>, C == D`, with x: D passed to A, is accepted by the baseline (0.8 s). With fixsubst AND with fixsubst,eqrefute it runs out of memory at the default cap. eqrefute gives up because one side is structured. c06 with fixsubst at cap 9 also runs out of memory.
issues.correction: The fix section's cost claim ('155 s to reject eqbug-1') understates the consequences. Programs with plain generic-parameter equalities, or with a structured side such as Box<B>, exhaust memory under fixsubst, and the structured case also does so under fixsubst,eqrefute. So the recommended configuration turns some wrong acceptances into compiler crashes.

issues.title: No second cause found among the other suspected paths
issues.evidence: I read the code. threadContinuation sets the environment to operand.substitutions, and operand always comes from the success path, which is env ∪ substitutions. applyContinuation unions both tables; on a conflict it overwrites, with only a debug assert, but fixsubst prevents conflicts from arising. formThread reifies under the environment. canDeriveCoercions is only a necessary-condition filter, called with the pre-unification environment, so it can cost completeness but cannot cause unsoundness. The coercememo key leaves out the substitutions, but coercememo is not in the baseline and is also only a filter. Pending premises used as candidates are discharged in LIFO order with dropLast, so I found no circularity. Empirically, every counterexample (c01, c03, c04, c06, c07, v03) is rejected under fixsubst at caps 7-10. c03 is rejected at cap 10 in 42 s.
issues.correction: None needed for the claim of a single cause, but the write-up could list the paths that were checked.

what_held: The trace of bug-assoc-eq-two-links.hylo matches the write-up's derivation exactly: transitivity<D.X, ?e, A.X>, then the given A.X~B.X coerced to (?e ~ A.X) assuming B.X~A.X (proved by symmetry), then reflexivity rebinds ?e := D.X.

The root cause is in Typer.match's coercion path: thread.environment.assuming(givens: gs) keeps the old substitutions and drops the ones the current unification produced, while the success path merges them with union.
Premise order (the last premise is discharged first) explains why ?e is bound by the given before reflexivity rebinds it.

Across the paths I checked by reading the code and testing every counterexample under fixsubst, I found no other path that drops substitutions (threadContinuation, applyContinuation, formThread, coerced, canDeriveCoercions memos, pending premises used as candidates).
Types that are unrelated, both not in any equality (c05) and on argument paths without equalities (v05, v06), are rejected by the baseline at caps 7-8; c05 runs out of memory at cap 10.
eqbug-5 / v07 (valid equalities) are accepted under both the baseline and fixsubst.

reviews.summary: The root cause and the `fixsubst` fix hold up. The baseline trace matches the write-up. `union` is safe because `formThread` reifies both sides first, and `fixsubst` rejected every ill-typed variant I tried (nested, three equalities, plain generic parameters). It accepted every valid program I tried that the baseline accepts. The `eqrefute` soundness claim is false: v-abs-7.hylo is a valid program that the baseline and `fixsubst` accept and `fixsubst,eqrefute` rejects. The write-up wrongly treats associated types as atoms that congruence cannot relate. An associated type with an abstract qualification (inside a trait) unifies through its qualification type, so resolution derives `(Self::P).X ~ U` from `T.X == U` and `T == Self`, while `eqrefute` refutes it.

issues.title: eqrefute rejects a valid program that the baseline and fixsubst accept (congruence through abstract-qualified associated types)
issues.correction: Remove 'associated types' from the list of atoms in the write-up's soundness argument, or qualify it. The claim 'coercions of one equality witness into another ... require proving equalities between the sides, i.e. again within the closure' is false when a side is an associated type with an abstract qualification: the required premise relates the qualification types. Fix in code: in equalityIsRefuted, bail out (return false) if a goal side or a fact side is an AssociatedType with an `.abstract` qualification. Alternatively, close the union-find under congruence of qualification types: merge (Q1::P).X and (Q2::P).X when Q1 and Q2 are in the same class and the unifier would relate them. Add v-abs-7.hylo as a positive test. The 192 tests and the standard library do not cover this: the stdlib has no equality given at all (grep finds none), and only 4 positive tests use '=='.

issues.title: eqrefute does not reify assumed givens, so most pending assumptions disable it, unlike the description
issues.evidence: From the code, not run. equalityIsRefuted collects `environment.givens` through declaredType(of: g). For `.assumed(i, t)` that returns t unreified (the canDeriveCoercions comment confirms `declaredType(of: .assumed(_, t)) == t`). The traces show pending assumptions such as '$1: (%dpd ~ %dpe)' whose variables are bound in the environment. atom() returns nil for any side with a variable, and the loop then does `return false` for the whole query. The extra effect is that it bails out more often, so this does not make it unsound.
issues.correction: Say that eqrefute gives up whenever an assumed given has a variable, even one already bound. Or reify assumed givens with environment.substitutions before the atom check, which would make the description ('including the assumed ones') accurate. Also note the code bails out on equality givens that have usings but no parameters, not only on 'quantified' equalities.

issues.title: No evidence in the repository that fixsubst alone rejects eqbug-1..4 at the default depth
issues.evidence: soundness/eqbug-results.txt records 'eqbug-N [fixsubst] diags= ms=TIMEOUT' for all four variants (run-eqbug.sh, timeout 600). The write-up says 'Rejects all four bug variants'. I ran HYLO_TC_MAXDEPTH=7: flags off accepts eqbug-1..4 (diags=0), fixsubst rejects them (diags=1, about 0.7-0.85 s each). At depth 6 the baseline already rejects eqbug-1, so the bug needs depth 7 or more.
issues.correction: Say that the rejection with fixsubst alone was observed at depth cap 7 (or cite the 155 s depth-10 run with its output saved). At default depth fixsubst alone times out or is very slow, as the performance section says. Mention that the bug needs a depth of at least 7, which matters for anyone using small caps.

issues.title: Union of substitution tables: conflicting bindings are only an assert, but they cannot occur
issues.evidence: From the code, not run. SubstitutionTable.union overwrites with `other`'s binding. It only asserts consistency, and the assert is disabled in release. match() unifies thread.witness.type with thread.queried into a fresh table. Every thread that reaches match comes from formThread, which reifies both witness and queried with environment.substitutions (Typer.swift 3790-3793), or from copy(matching:w,to:b), where the witness type equals queried. So no variable already bound in the environment can be rebound by the fresh unification. applyContinuation's union combines an extension of the elaboration's table, so it is consistent too.
issues.correction: The write-up could add one sentence on why union is safe: both sides are reified first, so the two tables bind disjoint variables. A precondition assert in match(), or a reify there, would make that explicit.

what_held: The root-cause description: Environment.assuming(givens:) keeps the old substitutions and drops the ones computed by the unification in match(). The impl10 trace of eqbug-1 with flags off at depth 7 matches the write-up's derivation exactly (transitivity with %dpe bound to A.X during one premise and to D.X through reflexivity in the other).

fixsubst rejects the ill-typed variants I built: eqbug-1..4, plain generic parameters (A == B, C == D; check<A>(x: D) and need<A, D>), three unrelated associated-type equalities, Box<D.X> passed as Box<A.X>, and the tuple {D.X, B.X} passed as {A.X, A.X}. The baseline accepts the eqbug and plain-parameter ones and fixsubst rejects them. The rest are rejected by every config at depth 7.

fixsubst and fixsubst,eqrefute accept every valid program I tried that the baseline accepts: associated-type-equality, conformance-via-equivalence, equality.hylo, coercion-derivability-cache (2.2 s in both configs), chains of length 2-3 with associated types, plain parameters and mixed directions at default depth, eqbug-5, aliases (type Q = S with T == Q, U == S), associated-type definitions (given S is P { type X = Bool }; T == S; need<T.X, Bool>), and congruence through abstract qualifications with value coercion (v-abs-2).
The bail-out conditions described for eqrefute appear in the code: open variables in the goal, a non-atom side in a fact, quantified or conditional equality givens, and a bare-variable head.
The union operation itself is appropriate: the tables bind disjoint variables because formThread reifies before matching.

verdict.reasoning:
I re-ran every major issue on the frozen binaries, with at most 2 processes at a time and timeout 300. My runner is /home/user/hylo-new/research/round3/soundness/review/eqsubst-judge/run.sh.

CAUSE. The mechanism is right. In Typer.match's coercion path, `thread.environment.assuming(givens: gs)` keeps the old substitutions and drops the ones the current unification computed (Typer.swift ~3874; the fixsubst branch follows it). The baseline trace of c01 shows the same bogus derivation as the write-up: transitivity<D, %e, V>, then the given V~W coerced to (%e ~ V) assuming W~V, then reflexivity rebinds %e := D. The write-up's description of which programs are affected is wrong, though.
- Results with base = 4587ce9e1a23, default depth:
  - c01 `g<D, V>()` with only V == W: 0 diagnostics.
  - c04 `g<D.X, A.X>()` with only A.X == B.X: 0.
  - c06 `g<Q, S>()` with only V == S, where Q is a concrete struct in no equality: 0.
  - c07, a value cast `h<D.X, A.X>(x)` with a single equality: 0.
  - c03, a given's premise `X == V` used to prove `D is P`: 0.
  - v02, plain generic parameters A == B, C == D: 0.
  - v03 `Box<D.X>` passed as `Box<A.X>`: 0.
- fixsubst,eqrefute rejects c01, c04, c06, c07 and v02, at about 0.6-0.8 s each.
- v01 (single equality, argument passing) is rejected by the baseline. That confirms that coerced()'s top-level `canDeriveCoercions(root.type, goal, ...)` pre-filter (Typer.swift 4357) is the only reason the repros need two equalities.
- So "types mentioned in no equality are still rejected" and "once two equalities are in scope" are false in general.

Depth claim. On impl10 with flags off, bug-assoc-eq-two-links and eqbug-1 are rejected at cap 6 and accepted at cap 7, so the bug needs a cap of at least 7. The baseline binary 4587ce9e1a23 ignores HYLO_TC_MAXDEPTH: there are no 'HYLO_TC_MAXDEPTH' strings in it, and it accepts at "3" and "6". So depth experiments must use impl10 with flags off.

FIX, fixsubst. It holds. The union of the two tables is safe because formThread reifies both sides first (I accept that from reading the code). eqbug-1 and eqbug-3 are rejected at cap 7, in about 1.4 s each. eqbug-results.txt records TIMEOUT (600 s) for all four under fixsubst at the default cap, and the 155 s rejection the write-up quotes has no saved output. The claim that fixsubst alone "rejects all four" therefore has to be qualified.

v02 under fixsubst alone, and v04 (`A == Box<B>, C == D`) under fixsubst,eqrefute, both abort at cap 10 with 'failed to allocate 402653240 bytes'. I checked why, and the reviewers did not: tc-bench is a wrapper script that sets `ulimit -v 2500000` (TCX_MEM_LIMIT_KB). This is exhaustion of a 2.5 GB harness cap, not an intrinsic compiler crash. It is still a resource blow-up instead of a fast rejection. v04 under fixsubst at cap 7 is rejected.

FIX, eqrefute. Its soundness claim is refuted. v-abs-7.hylo is a valid program:
```
trait P { type X; fun f<T, U where T == Self, T is P, T.X == U>() { need<X, U>() } }
```
It gets 0 diagnostics under the baseline, impl with flags off, and fixsubst, and 1 under fixsubst,eqrefute. The fixsubst trace is a genuine derivation: goal ((Self::P).X ~ U) <- $t : ((T::P).X ~ U), coerced assuming (T ~ Self), proved by $g. The cause is TypeStore.unifiable(AssociatedType, AssociatedType) (~1164). When either qualification is `.abstract`, it unifies the qualification types, so two associated types are related through an equality of their qualifications. equalityIsRefuted treats AssociatedType as an atom and uses plain unifiable without a coercion handler, so it never merges (Self::P).X with (T::P).X. This is a wrong rejection of a valid program, not a wrong acceptance. eqrefute exists only as a refutation shortcut, so it must not refute derivable goals.

The minor eqrefute issue checks out in the code. declaredType(of: .assumed(_, t)) returns t unreified (Typer.swift ~1741). An assumed given whose variables are already bound therefore makes atom() return nil, and the whole check gives up. That is conservative, not unsound. The code also gives up on equality givens that have usings (conditional ones), not only on quantified ones.

verdict.corrected_text:
## 1. Unrelated equalities make types interchangeable (unsound)

**Repro.** `soundness/bug-assoc-eq-two-links.hylo` and the variants `soundness/eqbug-1..4.hylo`:
```hylo
trait P { type X }
fun check<T>(x: T) {}
fun f<A, B, C, D where A is P, B is P, C is P, D is P, A.X == B.X, C.X == D.X>(x: D.X) {
  check<A.X>(x)   // accepted, but nothing relates A.X and D.X
}
```

**Which programs are affected.** The baseline proves an equality goal `L ~ R` whenever `R` is a side of some equality in scope.
- `L` can be any type when the goal is a call-site `where` requirement or a given's premise. That includes a type mentioned in no equality, or a concrete struct. Examples, with one equality each:
  - `fun f<V, W, D where V == W>() { g<D, V>() }`, where `g<T, U where T == U>`;
  - `fun f<V where V == S>() { g<Q, S>() }`;
  - `given <X where X == V> => X is P` proving `D is P`.
- When the goal comes from coercing an argument or annotation, `coerced()` first checks `canDeriveCoercions` on the outer pair. That check also requires `L` to be a side of some equality. This is why the repro above needs a second equality (`C.X == D.X`), and why the repro's comment "with a single equality the program is correctly rejected" holds only for that path.
- The sides can be generic parameters (`A == B, C == D`), associated types of unrelated traits (`D.Y`, eqbug-3), or nominal types.
- Types built from them are also interchangeable, for example `Box<D.X>` passed as `Box<A.X>`.
- The bogus derivation needs 7 resolution layers. At a depth cap of 6 or less, the program is rejected. When testing with small caps, use the impl binary with flags off: the frozen baseline binary ignores `HYLO_TC_MAXDEPTH`.

**The derivation the baseline accepts** (from the `trace` tool):
```
goal D.X ~ A.X  <- transitivity<T0 = D.X, T1 = ?e, T2 = A.X>
  premise ?e ~ A.X  <- the given A.X ~ B.X, coerced: unify (A.X ~ B.X) with (?e ~ A.X)
                        binds ?e := A.X, assumes B.X ~ A.X (proven by symmetry)
  premise D.X ~ ?e  <- reflexivity   (?e := D.X !)
result: transitivity<D.X, D.X, A.X>(reflexivity<D.X>)(coercion($A.X~B.X))(x)
```
The second premise is discharged last, because pending premises are discharged last-in, first-out.

**Root cause.** `Typer.match` (Typer.swift, "assume non-syntactic equalities between pairwise nested parts"):
- Unification of the witness's type with the goal records coercions for the parts that do not match.
- If those coercions may be derivable, it continues with `thread.environment.assuming(givens: gs)`. That environment **keeps the old substitutions and drops the `substitutions` that this very unification computed**.
- The success path (`coercions.isEmpty`) merges them correctly with `environment.substitutions.union(substitutions)`.

So a variable bound while proving one premise (`?e := A.X`) is free again when the next premise is proven, and can be bound to something else (`?e := D.X`).

Other paths checked, none of which drops substitutions:
- `threadContinuation`;
- `applyContinuation`;
- `formThread`, which reifies under the environment;
- `canDeriveCoercions`, which is only a necessary-condition filter.

**Fix (`fixsubst`).** Continue with `thread.environment.substitutions.union(substitutions)` in the coercion path as well.
- **Why `union` is safe.** `formThread` reifies both the witness and the query before matching, so the two tables bind disjoint variables.
- Identical on all 192 tests and on the standard library (same counters, no diagnostic).
- Rejects eqbug-1..4 at depth cap 7, in about 1.4 s each. At the default cap of 10 it is very slow: one run took 155 s and others exceeded 600 s (`eqbug-results.txt`).
- Rejects every other ill-typed variant tried: single equality, plain parameters, `Box<...>`, three equalities, and the generated `assocneg-N` workloads.
- Still accepts the valid control eqbug-5 (`B.X` used as `A.X` with `A.X == B.X`).

**Performance consequence.** With the bogus derivation gone, rejecting an ill-typed program means searching to the depth cap.
- eqbug-1 takes 3.3M matches and 155 s on an idle machine, and more than 600 s under load.
- Some ill-typed programs exceed the harness's 2.5 GB memory cap at the default depth instead of being rejected, for example `A == B, C == D` with `x: D` passed as `A`.

**Companion `eqrefute`** (meant to be used only together with `fixsubst`) restores fast rejection.
- **What it does.** Before searching for a closed equality goal `a ~ b` whose sides are atoms (generic parameters, associated types, or nominal types without arguments), it:
  1. collects the ground equality givens in scope, including the assumed ones;
  2. computes their equivalence classes with union-find, merging unifiable atoms;
  3. refutes the goal when `a` and `b` are in different classes.
- **When it gives up.**
  - a given can derive equalities from its own parameters: a quantified equality, a conditional equality (one with usings), or a `<T> T` head;
  - a fact has a structured side, where congruence could relate classes;
  - an assumed given still mentions variables, because assumed givens are not reified;
  - the goal has open variables.
- **It is not sound as implemented.** It rejects a valid program that the baseline and `fixsubst` both accept:
  ```hylo
  fun need<A, B where A == B>() {}
  trait P { type X; fun f<T, U where T == Self, T is P, T.X == U>() { need<X, U>() } }
  ```
  `fixsubst` derives `(Self::P).X ~ U` from `$t : (T::P).X ~ U` by a coercion that assumes `T ~ Self`. This works because unifying two associated types whose qualification is abstract unifies their qualification types (`TypeStore.unifiable(AssociatedType, AssociatedType)`).
- **Where the soundness argument fails.** The argument said that coercions between equality witnesses only require equalities between the sides, so every derivable equality lies within the closure. That is false for associated types: the premise can relate their qualifications. `equalityIsRefuted` treats associated types as atoms and never merges `(Self::P).X` with `(T::P).X`.
- **Required fix.** Give up when a side is an associated type with an abstract qualification, or close the union-find under qualification congruence. Add this program as a positive test, because the 192 tests do not cover it.
- **Also not handled.** With a structured side (`A == Box<B>, C == D`), `eqrefute` gives up, and the program still exceeds the memory cap.

Results:

| Program | Baseline | `fixsubst,eqrefute` |
|---|---|---|
| eqbug-1..4 | accepted (wrong), ≈1.4 s | rejected, ≈135 ms |
| assocneg-3 | accepted (wrong), 1.3 s | rejected, 133 ms |
| assocneg-8 | accepted (wrong), 4.4 s | rejected, 484 ms |
| single-equality call-site variants (`g<D, V>()`, `g<Q, S>()`) | accepted (wrong) | rejected, < 1 s |
| `A == Box<B>, C == D`, `x: D` as `A` | accepted (wrong) | exceeds the 2.5 GB memory cap |
| eqbug-5 (valid) | accepted, 140 ms | accepted, 137 ms |
| coercion-derivability-cache (valid) | accepted, 3.9 s | accepted, 3.9 s |
| `T == Self, T.X == U` ⊢ `X == U` (valid) | accepted | **rejected (wrong)** |

title: §2 Equality chains need an equality procedure (genuine search exponential once fixsubst is on)

reviews.summary: I tried to refute the claimed cause and could not. The baseline's proofs of valid equality chains are bogus. It finds them at a fixed size: 7 match layers for P<Tn> in trans-3, -4 and -5, and 7 for assoceq-4 and -5, whatever n is. Once fixsubst is on, the shortest genuine proof is the plain chain of coercions found by breadth-first search. It needs exactly 2n+2 layers for trans-n (n=2,3,4 give 6, 8, 10) and 2n+1 for assoceq-n (n=3,4 give 7, 9). Each layer explores about the same number of threads with and without fixsubst. So the slowdown is the search having to go deeper, not a fixsubst regression, and trans-5 (needs 12) and assoceq-5 (needs 11) are rejected only because they exceed the cap of 10. Three corrections: which links the chosen bogus proof skips; the "depth" cap actually bounds the total number of steps in a derivation, not its depth; and the genuine proofs use coerced matching of givens, not transitivity.

issues.title: The selected bogus trans-4 proof also uses T0~T1; only an unselected variant uses 'T2~T3 and T3~T4 alone'
issues.evidence: Ran: HYLO_TC_EXPERIMENTS=trace impl10 tc-bench --count trans-4.hylo (baseline, no fixsubst). P<T4> resolves at 7 layers with 2 completed derivations, both shaped transitivity<T0, ?e, T4>. Premise ?e~T4 comes from the given T2~T3 coerced, assuming only T3~T4; the binding ?e:=T2 is dropped. Premise T0~?e is then closed EITHER by the given $p: T0~T1 OR by reflexivity. Only the reflexivity variant uses just T2~T3 and T3~T4. The minimal one (lower penalty, since the visible given comes before the built-ins) uses $p. I confirmed this on assoceq-5, where the minimal witness is printed in full: 'penalty 6: coercion<T0.X,T5.X>(transitivity<T0.X, T1.X, T5.X>($1j)(coercion($27)))(x)'. It uses T0~T1, T3~T4 and T4~T5 and skips T1~T2 and T2~T3. The elaborated term is ill-typed: it coerces T3.X~T4.X to T1.X~T5.X having assumed only T4.X~T5.X. A third baseline derivation for assoceq-5 'proves' T5.X~T0.X from T0.X~T1.X alone, using reflexivity plus a coerced given.
issues.correction: Write: 'the baseline elaborates T0~T4 as transitivity<T0,T1,T4>(T0~T1)(coercion(T2~T3)), which skips T1~T2 (another derivation it finds uses only T2~T3 and T3~T4). Its bogus proofs have a fixed size of 7 layers whatever the chain length, which is why the baseline cost stays nearly flat.'

issues.title: The 'depth cap' bounds total derivation size, not tree depth; this is what makes trans-5 fail
issues.evidence: Code: takeSummonResults counts one layer per match() call. threadContinuation discharges pending premises one after another within the same thread, so a thread's layer count is the total number of matches in the whole derivation. A coercion step costs 2 (the coerced match, then a re-match). Measured minimum layer at which a resolution first completes (BFS, so this is the exact minimal size), the same for baseline and fixsubst where genuine: trans-2 P<T2> 5 and call 6; trans-3 P 7, call 8; trans-4 P 9 (28 derivations), call 10 (cap 9 gives diagnostics 1, cap 10 gives 0, 639,692 matches, matching the write-up's 640k). assoceq-3 needs 7 (cap 6 gives diagnostics 1, cap 7 gives 0). assoceq-4 needs 9: fixsubst at cap 8 gives diagnostics 1 (313,806 matches); at cap 9 diagnostics 0 (1.41M matches, 27 s, 1.6 GB RSS). Genuine proof shape from the trace: P<Tn> <- P<T0> coerced (2), then (Ti~Tn) <- given (Ti~Ti+1) coerced, assuming (Ti+1~Tn), 2 per link, last link 1, plus 1 for the call. Total 2n+2 for trans-n and 2n+1 for assoceq-n (x-coercion 1, symmetry 1, chain 2n-1). Lower bound: every link must be used, each costs at least 1 match, and every link but one also needs either a transitivity node or a coercion re-match (+1). Neither bogus nor genuine proofs ever needed a balanced tree, because size, not height, is what is capped.
issues.correction: State that the cap limits derivation size (number of match steps, with premises discharged sequentially). A chain of n needs 2n+2 steps for trans (12 for trans-5) and 2n+1 for assoceq (11 for assoceq-5). So with fixsubst, trans-5 and assoceq-5 are correctly rejected by the cap; this is not a fixsubst bug. The write-up's 'timeout' for assoceq-5 would end in rejection, not acceptance, under the default cap. trans-8 needs 18.

issues.title: Genuine proofs are coerced matches of givens, not symmetry/transitivity search
issues.evidence: fixsubst trace for trans-4 (cap 10): goal (T0~T4) <- given T0~T1, coerced, assuming (T1~T4); (T1~T4) <- T1~T2 coerced; (T2~T4) <- T2~T3 coerced; (T3~T4) <- given. No transitivity node is used. assoceq adds one symmetry step because the goal direction is T3.X~T0.X. Transitivity and symmetry only widen the branching factor (transitivity matches any equality goal and introduces fresh variables).
issues.correction: Say the genuine search is 'breadth-first search over all givens with coercion-based congruence, plus the symmetry/transitivity built-ins'. The shortest proof is a linear chain of coercions, so its length grows linearly with n, and the number of nodes searched grows exponentially in that length.

issues.title: No fixsubst regression in the explored search space
issues.evidence: Same caps, baseline vs fixsubst, user match counts: trans-4 cap 6: 5,618 vs 5,618. trans-4 cap 7: 21,894 vs 21,821 (baseline finds 2 bogus proofs, fixsubst finds 0). trans-3 cap 8: 29,801 vs 29,655. assoceq-3 cap 7: 60,438 vs 59,664. fixsubst only removes the threads that relied on a dropped binding. The extra cost comes entirely from having to search more layers (roughly x4-5 per layer).
issues.correction: None needed; the write-up could add this evidence.

issues.title: Tooling caveat: trace runs out of memory on large searches
issues.evidence: Ran HYLO_TC_MAXDEPTH=9 HYLO_TC_EXPERIMENTS=fixsubst,trace on assoceq-4. It aborted with 'Fatal error: failed to allocate 217595712 bytes'. Every thread carries its own copy of the log. The same run without trace succeeded (1.6 GB peak).
issues.correction: Note that trace is only usable with small caps or small n.

what_held: The baseline's proofs of valid chains are bogus because of the binding dropped on the coercion path in Typer.match. Traces of trans-3, -4, -5 and assoceq-5 show transitivity<T0, ?e, Tn> where ?e is bound while coercing one premise and then rebound by T0~T1 or reflexivity in the other.
For trans-4 the baseline proof skips links: T1~T2 is never used, and P<T4> resolves at 7 layers. The genuine proof needs 9.
For trans-3 the genuine and bogus proofs have the same size (7). That explains why baseline and fixsubst cost the same there (29.8k vs 29.7k matches).

With fixsubst the cost grows exponentially with chain length: about 2.3k, 30k and 640k matches for trans-2, -3, -4. This is because the required size grows linearly (2n+2) and each layer multiplies the work by about 4-5.
With fixsubst, the rejection of trans-5 at the default cap is a cap effect (it needs 12 layers, the cap is 10). It is not a fixsubst bug: the pattern 2n+2 holds exactly for n=2,3,4.
The trans-4 fixsubst figure of 640k matches reproduces exactly (639,692).

issues.title: Chains of 5+ links are rejected by the depth cap no matter how fast the search is; 'exponential in chain length' misplaces the cause of rejection
issues.evidence: Ran: run.sh impl10 fixsubst with HYLO_TC_MAXDEPTH=4..10. Smallest cap that accepts each program: trans-2 needs 6, trans-3 needs 8, trans-4 needs 10 (2n+2); transconf-2/3/4 need 6/8/10 (2n); assoceq-2 needs at most 5 and assoceq-3 needs 7 (2n+1). The trace of trans-4 shows why: each link costs one match layer ('coerce (T1~T2) to (T1~T4) assuming T2~T4') plus one discharge layer ('now prove $3'). So with the default cap of 10, trans-5 (needs 12), transconf-5 (12), assoceq-5 (11) and trans-8 (18) are rejected by construction. The baseline accepts trans-4, trans-5 and trans-8 at cap 8 regardless of length (its proofs are bogus and do not grow with the chain). Cost is exponential in the depth reached, about 4.4x per layer: trans-4 at cap 8/9/10 = 90k/392k/640k matches. trans-5 with fixsubst at cap 10 and the memory limit raised: 51 s, 2.2M matches, depthExhausted=2, 3 diagnostics.
issues.correction: Say that a genuine proof needs about 2 layers per link, so with the default cap of 10, fixsubst rejects chains of 5 or more links outright: it is a completeness cliff, not only a slowdown. The exponential cost is base^(2n), and it also makes chains of 3 and 4 links slow (trans-4 takes 13-20 s). Any remedy that keeps proving equalities as same-thread search subgoals keeps the cliff. The procedure must answer an equality subgoal in a single step, or take equality subproofs out of the depth count.

issues.title: With the frozen binary's memory cap, 'timeout' is in fact an out-of-memory crash
issues.evidence: Ran: impl10 tc-bench (a wrapper that sets ulimit -v 2.5 GB) with fixsubst on trans-5, trans-8, assoceq-5 and openchain-5 (pick(a,b) across 5 equalities). All exit with rc=134 'Fatal error: failed to allocate 828440512 bytes' in Typer.takeSummonResults (Typer.swift:3973, Array.append of the BFS frontier). trans-8 and assoceq-5 both crash within 35 s wall. Only with TCX_MEM_LIMIT_KB=12000000 did trans-5 finish (51 s, rejected).
issues.correction: Report that fixsubst alone turns these valid programs into compiler crashes under the standard memory limit, not just into rejections or timeouts, because the BFS frontier grows exponentially in memory as well. That strengthens the 'land together' recommendation.

issues.title: eqrefute is a fragile special case, not 'the negative half': one unrelated structured equality in scope disables it
issues.evidence: Ran: eqbug1-struct.hylo is eqbug-1 with two unrelated parameters and the clause 'Box<Z> == W' added. fixsubst,eqrefute on the plain eqbug-1: rejected in 102 ms, refuted=1. On eqbug1-struct: rc=134 out-of-memory crash at 2.5 GB; with 10 GB, 108 s, 4.6M matches, refuted=0, 1 diagnostic. Baseline: accepts wrongly in 1 s. Cause in the code: equalityIsRefuted returns false as soon as any visible given has a non-atom side ('guard let l = atom(...) ... else { return false }'), or has a context or a bare-variable head.
issues.correction: Describe eqrefute as the atom-only, all-or-nothing special case. It gives up for every goal in a scope that contains any structured, conditional or quantified equality, wherever that equality appears. A real negative half needs congruence closure over structured terms, so that unrelated facts do not disable it.

issues.title: The theory is under-specified: the engine poses decomposed subgoals that need injectivity, which congruence closure does not provide
issues.evidence: Ran: decomp-2.hylo `fun f<A, B where Box<A> == Box<B>, Box<A> is P>() { need<Box<B>>() }` is rejected by the baseline, by fixsubst and by fixsubst,eqrefute ('no coercion ...'; the trace shows 'resolve P<Box<B>>: 1 layers, 0 done'). match unifies P<Box<A>> with P<Box<B>>, records the innermost mismatch (A, B) and asks for A ~ B. Congruence closure of {Box<A> = Box<B>} does not contain A = B; deriving it takes decomposition (injectivity of a nominal constructor). In contrast, decomp-1 (x: Box<A> passed as Box<B> under the same equality) is accepted. quant-4 (Box<A>==C, Box<B>==D, C==D, so A ~ B) is also rejected by all configurations.
issues.correction: Specify the procedure as congruence closure plus decomposition/injectivity of nominal type constructors (and clash detection for refutation), or have match pose coercions at the outermost mismatching level. Otherwise the decomposed nested-part coercions that match produces are not decided by the closure.

issues.title: The `canDeriveCoercions` pre-filter blocks congruence-derivable goals before any search, so the remedy must replace it too
issues.evidence: Ran: quant-2c.hylo `fun f<A, B, C where C == Box<A>, A == B>(x: C) { check<Box<B>>(x) }` is rejected by the baseline and by fixsubst with summon.matches=1 and no subgoals (also quant-2 with the facts written the other way round). canDeriveCoercion (Typer.swift around line 4476) requires each side of the queried pair to unify with a side of some equality given. Box<B> appears in no given, so the coercion is refused without search, although C = Box<A> = Box<B> follows by congruence. quant-2b (no A == B step) is accepted.
issues.correction: Say that the equality procedure has to replace the 'may a coercion be derivable' test in canDeriveCoercions and coerced, not only the SLD search over the reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity givens. Otherwise valid congruence goals never reach it. Answering that test by class membership would also be cheaper.

issues.title: Associated types must stay opaque, keyed by their conformance witness; naive congruence on T.X would be unsound
issues.evidence: negative/associated-type-inequality.hylo requires that T == U, T is P, U is P does NOT give (T::P).X == (U::P).X. A congruence closure that treats T.X as a function X(T) would accept it. In practice name resolution already canonicalizes: in cong-1.hylo (T == U, T is P, V == U.X) the trace shows the fact as (V ~ (T::P).X), and cong-0/1/2 are accepted by all configurations.
issues.correction: State that the function symbols for congruence are the nominal type constructors only. Associated types are atoms identified by their qualifying witness term, and any congruence on witnesses (for example coercion(T0::P)) must be defined explicitly.

issues.title: Open goals: 'unify against class representatives' is imprecise and may change inferred substitutions
issues.evidence: Not run as a separate test. From code reading: takeSummonResults keeps the minimal-penalty results of the first successful layer, and given equalities have a lower penalty group than the builtin reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity givens. So for ?x ~ T4 the current engine prefers ?x := T3 from a fact over ?x := T4 from reflexivity. Picking a union-find representative selects differently. A goal with structure and repeated variables (for example Pair<?x, ?x> ~ Pair<A, B> with A == B) is rigid E-unification modulo ground equations, which is NP-complete in general; it is not a single unification against a representative. open-1..4 (pick(a, d) across 1-3 equalities) are accepted by all configurations; openchain-4 takes 5.4 s with fixsubst and openchain-5 crashes out of memory.
issues.correction: Say that open goals need unification followed by a closure check (unify syntactically, collect the mismatched pairs as closure queries), and that inferred substitutions, not only proof terms, may change. That is an observable semantic change to validate with the oracle.

issues.title: Cheaper options inside the current engine: they can cut the cost but cannot fix the cliff, and the existing flags barely help
issues.correction: Add that the existing flags give at most a 2x improvement. A cheap interim option is a positive counterpart to eqrefute (a closed goal between atoms in one class is proved directly from the union-find path), and it needs no new machinery. Any search-based option must also exempt equality subproofs from the depth cap.

what_held: Baseline proofs of valid chains do not scale with chain length (bogus): with the baseline, trans-4, trans-5 and trans-8 are all accepted at cap 8, and only trans-4 and later are fast.
With fixsubst, trans-3 costs the same as the baseline (29,655 vs 29,801 matches), and trans-4 jumps to 640k matches and 12.8 s (the write-up says 19.7 s; that is load variance).
trans-5 with fixsubst at cap 10 is rejected after exhausting the depth (51 s with memory raised, 2.2M matches; the write-up says 79 s).
fixsubst alone makes chains longer than 4 unusable: confirmed, and in fact understated (depth cliff and out-of-memory crashes).
A decision procedure, not search, is needed for completeness under the depth cap: confirmed, because every same-thread search proof costs 2 layers per link.
eqrefute rejects the negative chain workloads quickly when every equality in scope is atom-to-atom (eqbug-1: 102 ms; transneg-3/5/8 and assocneg-5 are fast).
The minimal derivation chosen for trans-4 is the plain chain of given facts, which matches the write-up's picture of what a correct proof should look like.

verdict.reasoning:
I re-ran every major claim with the frozen impl10 binary, at most 2 processes at a time. My outputs are in /home/user/hylo-new/research/round3/soundness/review/eqchain-judge/.

The cause holds.
- The baseline's proofs of valid chains are bogus. My baseline trace of trans-4 (base-trans4-trace.txt) shows P<T4> resolved at 7 layers with 2 derivations, both shaped transitivity<T0, ?e, T4>. Premise ?e~T4 comes from the given T2~T3, coerced, assuming T3~T4. Premise T0~?e is then closed either by $p (T0~T1) or by reflexivity. So T1~T2 is never used. "From T2~T3 and T3~T4 alone" is true of only one of the two derivations.
- The baseline cost is nearly flat: 35k matches for trans-4, 41k for trans-5 at cap 10.
- With fixsubst: trans-3 has 29,655 matches and needs cap 8 (cap 7 gives a diagnostic). trans-4 has 639,692 matches, 13.6 s, and needs cap 10 (cap 9: diagnostic, 392k matches). That fits a genuine proof costing 2 layers per link, because takeSummonResults advances every thread one match per layer and premises are discharged one after another. The cap therefore bounds the size of a derivation, not its depth.
- Hence trans-5 (12 layers needed) and assoceq-5 (11) cannot succeed at cap 10, however fast the search is. The write-up says "exponential", which is true of the cost, but rejection is a hard cliff caused by the cap.
- Under the binary's standard 2.5 GB limit, trans-5, trans-8 and assoceq-5 with fixsubst abort with rc=134 (out of memory) after about 35 s. They do not take ">120 s"; the write-up's 79 s / rejected figure for trans-5 needs a raised memory limit.

The fix direction is right but under-specified. I confirmed:
- (a) eqbug1-struct (eqbug-1 plus one unrelated `Box<Z> == W`): fixsubst,eqrefute runs out of memory (rc=134), whereas eqbug-1 alone is refuted in 70 ms. The cause is in equalityIsRefuted, which returns false as soon as any visible given has a non-atom side. So eqrefute is an all-or-nothing atom-only special case, not "the negative half" of a procedure.
- (b) decomp-2 (needs A~B from Box<A>==Box<B>) and quant-4 are rejected by the baseline and every config. Congruence closure alone does not derive the decomposed subgoals that match poses; the procedure also needs injectivity/decomposition of nominal constructors.
- (c) quant-2 and quant-2c are rejected after 1 match and no subgoals in all configs, while quant-2b is accepted. canDeriveCoercion asks that each side unify with a side of some equality given, so congruence-derivable goals are filtered out before any search runs. The procedure must replace that pre-filter too.
- (d) negative/associated-type-inequality.hylo requires associated types to stay opaque, keyed by their conformance. So congruence must treat T.X as an atom, not as a function of T.
- (e) Existing flags do not remove the blow-up: on trans-4, loopcheck gives 336,736 matches (about 2x fewer) and eqrefute leaves the count identical at 639,692.

What I accepted with less evidence:
- The open-goal concern is accepted on argument only. Matching structured goals with repeated variables modulo ground equations is rigid E-unification, so "unify against class representatives" is imprecise. I did not verify that inferred substitutions change, so that part is not included.
- Which of the two baseline derivations is minimal is left unstated. Likewise which of the 28 genuine trans-4 derivations wins: the trace shows both transitivity-node and coerced-fact chains, all at 2 layers per link.

verdict.corrected_text:
## 2. Equality chains need an equality procedure, not search

Bug #1 also explains why valid equality chains were "fast". The baseline's proofs of them are bogus, with the right conclusion by luck. For `trans-4`, `T0 ~ T4` is "proved" without ever using `T1 ~ T2`: `transitivity<T0, ?e, T4>` proves `?e ~ T4` by coercing `T2 ~ T3` (assuming `T3 ~ T4`), and then, through the same dropped binding, closes `T0 ~ ?e` by reflexivity or by `T0 ~ T1`. These bogus proofs have a fixed size (about 7 match steps, 8 for the call) whatever the chain length, so the baseline cost stays nearly flat.

With `fixsubst`, every proof is genuine, and a genuine proof costs about **2 match steps per link**: 2n+2 for trans-n, 2n+1 for assoceq-n. The resolution "depth" cap bounds the **size** of a derivation, not its height: each BFS layer advances every thread by one match, and pending premises are discharged one after another. Each extra step multiplies the work by about 4-5:

| Chain | Baseline (bogus proof) | `fixsubst` (genuine search) |
|---|---|---|
| trans-3 | 731 ms, 30k matches | 745 ms, 30k matches (needs cap 8) |
| trans-4 | 918 ms, 35k matches | **13-20 s, 640k matches** (needs cap 10; cap 9 rejects) |
| trans-5 | 1.2 s, 41k matches | needs 12 steps, so rejected by the default cap of 10. Under the standard 2.5 GB limit it **crashes out of memory** (about 35 s). With the limit raised: 51-79 s, rejected |
| assoceq-5, trans-8 | 2.7 s / 1.9 s | need 11 and 18 steps. **Out-of-memory crash** after about 35 s |

The search space explored per layer is the same with and without `fixsubst` (for example trans-3 at cap 8: 29.8k vs 29.7k matches). The slowdown comes entirely from having to go deeper. The existing performance flags do not change this: on trans-4, `loopcheck` halves the matches (337k) and `eqrefute` leaves them unchanged (640k).

**Conclusion.** `fixsubst` alone is correct but makes the equality fragment unusable:
- chains of 3-4 links become slow;
- chains of 5 or more links are rejected outright by the cap, or crash the compiler, however fast the search is.

Equalities need a decision procedure that answers an equality subgoal in one step, instead of SLD search with built-in symmetry and transitivity givens. Requirements on that procedure:
- **Theory.** Congruence closure over the equalities in scope, **plus decomposition (injectivity) of nominal type constructors**. `match` poses the innermost mismatched parts as subgoals. For example, `Box<A> == Box<B>, Box<A> is P` needs `A ~ B` to use `P<Box<B>>`, and congruence alone does not give that (`decomp-2`, `quant-4` are rejected today in every configuration). Clash detection between distinct constructors gives the negative answers.
- **Atoms.** Associated types are opaque atoms identified by their qualifying conformance witness, not functions of their base type. `T == U` must not give `T.X == U.X` (`negative/associated-type-inequality.hylo`).
- **Pre-filter.** It must also replace the "may a coercion be derivable" test in `canDeriveCoercions`/`coerced`. That test requires each side to unify with a side of some equality given, so it rejects congruence-derivable goals before any search: `C == Box<A>, A == B` with `x: C` used as `Box<B>` is rejected after 1 match (`quant-2`, `quant-2c`).
- **Ground goals.** Union-find decides `a ~ b` and produces the proof term from the path.
- **Open goals.** Unify syntactically, then check the mismatched pairs against the closure. In general this is rigid E-unification, not a single unification against a class representative, so validate any change in inferred bindings with the oracle.

This is a design change: the proof terms change, and equality subproofs no longer count toward the depth cap. It should land together with `fixsubst`. `eqrefute` above is only a narrow first step towards the negative half. It works only when **every** equality in scope is between atoms, and it gives up for all goals as soon as any structured, conditional or quantified equality is visible, even an unrelated one. For example, eqbug-1 plus an unrelated `Box<Z> == W` is no longer refuted, and with `fixsubst,eqrefute` it crashes out of memory (`review/eqchain-fix/eqbug1-struct.hylo`).

title: §3 where T.X == B at a call site is never discharged (incompleteness + blow-up)

reviews.summary: The repro is real: `f2<A>()` is rejected, and the immediate symptom is as described, since `(A::P).X ~ B` cannot be reduced to `B ~ B`. But the cause in §3 is mislocated and too narrow. The qualification is not "abstract". It is a reference to the callee's own where-clause binding (`T is P`) with T replaced by A. The defect is in how a generic signature is instantiated, not in how a second requirement is summoned, so a call fails even when `T.X` appears only in a parameter or return type with no equality requirement. The order in which premises are discharged plays no part in the current failure, the sentence "eqrefute does not apply" is false as measured, and "never discharged" has exceptions.

issues.title: Defect is not specific to `where T.X == B` or to summoning the second requirement: any use of T.X in an instantiated signature fails
issues.evidence: Ran on both impl10-37a7007e33a0 and the baseline 4587ce9e1a23 (default cap and cap 5). v3-param.hylo has `fun f3<T where T is P>(x: T.X) {}` with `f3<A>(B())` and gives "error: cannot pass value of type 'B' to parameter '(A::P).X'". v7-ret.hylo has `fun f6<T where T is P>() -> T.X` with `let y: B = f6<A>()` and gives "error: no coercion from '(A::P).X' to 'B'". Both fail fast (about 18 ms) and no equality premise is involved. `let y: A.X = B()` (v8-proj) is accepted.
issues.correction: Restate the cause like this. When a generic signature is instantiated, `f<A>` substitutes A for T but leaves each associated type's qualification witness pointing at the callee's own where-clause binding. Nothing maps that reference to the witness that resolution finds for P<A>. That affects the head (parameter and return types) as well as later premises. The proposed fix, "substitute each witness into later requirements", does not cover the head: in `coerced`/`formThread` the head is matched before any premise is discharged. Only the second alternative (normalize `(A::P).X` through a summoned P<A> conformance at instantiation) would fix v3 and v7. Either widen §3's title and scope, or say explicitly that the equality case is one instance.

issues.title: Wrong qualification: it is a reference to the callee's where-clause binding, not an abstract witness, and the printer hides the difference
issues.evidence: I read the code; this was not an execution. In Parser.swift, a where-clause `T is P` becomes `synthesizeUsingDeclaration`, a given binding. Summoning P<T> in f2's scope gives `expression(referringTo:)`, which is `.reference(implicit var of that binding)`. That is not a ConformanceDeclaration, so `typeOfImplementation(satisfying:in:)` (Typer.swift ~3352) takes the opaque branch and builds `AssociatedType(X, qualification: ref(using) : P<T>)`. Instantiation only substitutes types. `AssociatedType.show` prints `(\(a.values[0])::\(m)).X`, the trait arguments only, so qualifications with different witnesses print the same. Execution evidence: v5-generic.hylo has `fun h<U where U is P, U.X == B>() { f2<U>() }`. Under fixsubst,eqrefute it is rejected, with eqrefute.refuted=2, even though h's given `(U::P).X ~ B` is in scope. eqrefute merges unifiable atoms, so f2's `(U::P).X` and h's `(U::P).X` must be distinct types.
issues.correction: Replace "summoned with an abstract qualification A::P" with "the qualification is `ref(<callee's using binding>) : P<A>`, a free reference to the callee's context parameter that is out of scope at the call site". Note that diagnostics and traces print these qualifications identically, so `(A::P).X` in an error message proves nothing about which witness it holds.

issues.title: Order of discharge does not cause the current bug (it only matters for the fix)
issues.evidence: Code: `formThread` assumes the premises in order (`assuming(given:)` appends), and `threadContinuation` pops `givens.last`. So in `(P<A>, (A::P).X ~ B) ==> ...` the equality ($1) is proven before P<A> ($0). But the type of $1 never mentions `.assumed(0)`: it mentions the callee's binding reference. Neither order would reduce it, and v3/v7 fail with no second premise at all.
issues.correction: Say that the dependency is not represented at all: later premises and the head reference the callee's binding, not the earlier premise's placeholder. Discharging in reverse order is an additional obstacle for the proposed fix, which would need forward order or deferred normalization. It is not the cause.

issues.title: "`eqrefute` does not apply" is false: it refutes the goal and removes the blow-up
issues.evidence: Ran `--count min.hylo` on impl10. At cap 5: no flags gives user summon.matches=7094, eqrefute gives 292. At default cap 10 under eqrefute (and under fixsubst,eqrefute): eqrefute.refuted=2, summon.matches=292, type.user 24-29 ms, and a clean "no coercion" error instead of running out of memory. Both sides are atoms (AssociatedType and Struct) in different classes, which is exactly the refutation condition. The write-up's own reason ("unifiable with nothing in scope") is the reason eqrefute does apply.
issues.correction: Say that with `eqrefute` the blow-up disappears: rejection is immediate at any cap. The incompleteness remains, because eqrefute refutes a true equality that this procedure cannot derive.

issues.title: "Never discharged" is overstated
issues.evidence: v6-refl.hylo has `fun f5<T where T is P, T.X == T.X>()` with `f5<A>()` and gives diagnostics: 0 (reflexivity). In a generic caller (v5) the baseline with no flags, at default cap, accepts `f2<U>()` (diagnostics: 0, 1.6 s). The trace shows a penalty-17 derivation through symmetry and transitivity with an unbound middle variable %dj5, which is the bug #1 path. With fixsubst alone it runs out of memory (allocation failure in takeSummonResults). With fixsubst,eqrefute it is rejected.
issues.correction: Say "never discharged except by reflexivity or through the unsound bug #1 path". Add the generic-caller case: the baseline accepts it only via #1; it is rejected once #1 is fixed, and fixsubst alone runs out of memory. So fixing #1 turns an accidental acceptance into a rejection or a blow-up.

issues.title: Order of where-clauses: swapping it produces a different, earlier error
issues.evidence: v2-swapped.hylo has `fun f2<T where T.X == B, T is P>()` and gives "error: type 'T' has no static member 'X'" at the declaration, then the call fails with a premise `#!`. Name resolution of T.X only sees usings declared earlier.
issues.correction: This could be mentioned as a separate limitation. It does not offer another way to discharge the requirement.

what_held: The minimized repro is valid-looking Hylo and is rejected. Under trace, the call's type is `(P<A>, ((A::P).X ~ B)) ==> [Void]() let -> Void`, and the P<A> premise is found as the given `A is P` (ConformanceDeclaration at min:4.1).
Associated-type projection on a concrete type works: `let y: A.X = B()` has 0 diagnostics.
Without eqrefute the equality goal makes the search explode with depth: 7094 user matches at cap 5 on impl10 with no flags, consistent with the reported growth.

The second alternative fix (normalize associated types with concrete qualifications through the conformance) points in the right direction, and it is the only one of the two proposed fixes that also covers parameter and return types.

No positive compiler test exercises a concrete call to a function whose signature mentions T.X (associated-type-equality.hylo only uses them inside the generic body), so the gap is untested rather than contradicted by an existing passing test.

reviews.summary: The symptom in §3 reproduces, but the stated cause is too narrow and partly mislabelled, and the proposed remedy would not be enough. The real defect is broader: when a generic callee's signature is instantiated, the qualification of every associated-type projection is a reference to the callee's own `using` declaration, and nothing ever substitutes it. That breaks parameter types and abstract (generic) callers too, not just `where T.X == B` with a concrete T. Neither proposed fix covers all the failing cases. Separately, the claim that `eqrefute` does not apply is refuted: `eqrefute` refutes the goal and removes the blow-up.

issues.title: Scope too narrow: the defect is not specific to where-clause equalities; associated-type projections in parameter and result types fail too
issues.evidence: Ran on both binaries. t3-param.hylo: `fun h<T where T is P>(x: T.X) {}` with `h<A>(B())`, where `given A is P { type X = B }`. Baseline and impl both give 'error: cannot pass value of type 'B' to parameter '(A::P).X''. t6-ret.hylo (same h, returning T.X) gives 'no coercion from '(A::P).X' to 'B''. Neither program has an equality requirement.
issues.correction: Restate the defect: when a generic signature is instantiated, a projection `T.X` keeps the qualification `.reference(<callee's using decl for T is P>)`. typeOfImplementation (the only routine that reduces a projection) runs only during name resolution, so `(A::P).X` is never reduced anywhere in the instantiated callee type: parameters, result, or later requirements. 'Substitute each witness into the later requirements' does not reach the parameter types in t3 and t6. The substitution has to apply to the whole instantiated callee type, and before the argument constraints are solved.

issues.title: Fix is insufficient for generic (abstract) callers; the 'concrete qualification' alternative does nothing there
issues.evidence: t4-generic-caller.hylo: `fun f2<T where T is P, T.X == B>() {}` and `fun g<U where U is P, U.X == B>() { f2<U>() }`. t12: `fun h<T where T is P>(x: T.X) {}` and `fun g<U where U is P>(y: U.X) { h<U>(y) }` gives 'cannot pass value of type '(U::P).X' to parameter '(U::P).X'' on both binaries. TypeStore.unifiable(AssociatedType, AssociatedType) requires one qualification to be `.abstract`; here the two values are references to h's and g's using declarations, so they never unify.
issues.correction: Drop 'with concrete T' from the title and the description. Make the primary fix the substitution of the callee's using-declaration references by the argument witnesses (dependent requirements), not normalization with concrete qualifications. The alternative fixes neither t4 nor t12. The substitution is also not a matter of order alone: Implication stores only the usings' types (introduce(types:usings:) maps each using to declaredType), so nothing links the using in position 0 to the declaration `$i` that the later qualification refers to. That link has to be added.

issues.title: 'eqrefute does not apply' is false: eqrefute refutes the goal and removes the blow-up
issues.evidence: Ran impl10 on t1.hylo (the minimal repro). With no flags: cap 5 gives 7094 matches, cap 7 gives 80224 matches / 1.3 s. With fixsubst alone at cap 10: 'Fatal error: failed to allocate'. With eqrefute alone at cap 10: 'eqrefute.refuted=2 summon.matches=292 diagnostics: 1', 29 ms. fixsubst,eqrefute is the same at caps 5, 7 and 10. equalityIsRefuted treats AssociatedType as an atom. '(A::P).X is unifiable with nothing in scope' is exactly the condition that makes it refute.
issues.correction: Say that eqrefute turns the out-of-memory blow-up into a fast (still incorrect) rejection. Also warn that eqrefute currently refutes a TRUE equality ((A::P).X is B), because it does not normalize projections. Any normalization fix must run before equalityIsRefuted, or eqrefute keeps rejecting the program.

issues.title: eqrefute (and fixsubst) reject a valid generic-caller program that the baseline accepts
issues.evidence: semtest --bin impl10-37a7007e33a0 --configs eqrefute on t4-generic-caller.hylo reports MISMATCH: '+diag ... error: no coercion from '(P<U>, ((U::P).X ~ B)) ==> [Void]() let -> Void' ...'. Baseline (no flags, cap 10) has 0 diagnostics but 90983 matches. Its trace shows the derivation trans<(U::P).X,(U::P).X,B>(refl)(sym(coerce($y))), where coerce($y) turns (U::P).X ~ B into (B ~ %dj4), which needs the dropped binding %dj4:=B (bug #1). fixsubst at cap 10 runs out of memory.
issues.correction: Record in §3, or in the eqrefute and fixsubst sections, that the baseline accepts this valid pattern only through bug #1's bogus proof. Landing fixsubst/eqrefute without the §3 fix makes a generic function unable to call another generic function with an associated-type equality requirement. That reinforces Recommendation 2/3 ordering: the §3 fix has to land with them.

issues.title: Qualification mislabelled as 'abstract'
issues.evidence: The trace shows 'resolve P<T>: ... penalty 0: $i' when T.X is resolved in the where clause. WitnessExpression.show prints `.abstract` as '$<abstract given>' and `.reference(d)` by the declaration's name. The qualification is therefore `.reference(<f2's using decl>)`, not `.abstract`. The pretty printer hides the difference: both `(U::P).X` shown in t4's trace print identically but do not unify.
issues.correction: Write 'a qualification that refers to the callee's own (unbound) context parameter', not 'abstract qualification'. The distinction matters because unifiable(AssociatedType) treats `.abstract` as a wildcard, and these references are not.

issues.title: Requirements are currently discharged last-first; the write-up does not say so
issues.evidence: formThread pushes usings in order, and threadContinuation discharges `environment.givens.last` first. t4 trace: 'now prove $1: ((U::P).X ~ B) [pending: $0: P<U>]' ... and only at the end 'now prove $0: P<U> [pending: ]'.
issues.correction: State that the equality is resolved BEFORE the conformance it depends on. 'Resolve in order' means reversing the LIFO discharge. A pending goal's type must then be rewritten when $0 is solved: today applyContinuation substitutes assumed givens only in result witnesses, never in the types of pending goals.

issues.title: Normalizing through the found witness fails for generic and conditional conformances
issues.evidence: t13: `given <T> => Box<T> is P { type X = B }` with `let y: Box<B>.X = B()` gives 'expression does not denote a type'. t11 (X = T) behaves the same, and so does t7 (conditional `given <T is Q> => Box<T> is P`), on both binaries. t8 (f2<Box<B>>() with the conditional conformance) runs out of memory on the baseline. typeOfImplementation(satisfying:in:) only does `declaredType(of: implementation)` for the ConformanceDeclaration found through witness.declaration, without applying the witness's type arguments.
issues.correction: The claim that `(A::P).X` becomes `(A::<given A is P>).X = B` holds only for non-generic conformances. Both remedies also need typeOfImplementation (and aliasesInConformance) fixed to instantiate the conformance's generic parameters from the witness (typeApplication/termApplication arguments). Without that, projections through `given <T> => Box<T> is P` stay unreduced, and are mis-typed even at name resolution.

issues.title: Where-clause order: the difference is a declaration-site error, not a discharge-order effect
issues.evidence: t2-swapped: `fun f2<T where T.X == B, T is P>()` gives 't2-swapped.hylo:5.18-19: error: type 'T' has no static member 'X'', and the call type becomes '(#!, P<A>) ==> ...' (fast; same on the baseline). initializeContext hides later usings while it types earlier ones.
issues.correction: If the write-up or the review cites order dependence, attribute it to left-to-right scoping of where clauses at the declaration. The call-site fix does not change it.

issues.title: Coherence with multiple conformances: no divergence observed
issues.evidence: t9: outer `given A is P { type X = B }` and inner `given A is P { type X = C }` with `let y: A.X = C()` gives 0 diagnostics: the inner given wins by penalty. An independent re-summon of P<A> for normalization would pick the same witness in the same scope. I could not build a program where that summon and requirement 1 disagree without implementing the fix.
issues.correction: Prefer the dependent-substitution fix on principle: it uses exactly the witness that was passed. Normalizing by re-summoning is coherent only when the summon is deterministic and runs in the same scope. That should be stated as an assumption.

what_held: The minimal repro t1 is rejected; at cap 7 it takes 80k matches. The baseline at cap 10 runs out of memory (the baseline binary ignores HYLO_TC_MAXDEPTH, so it always runs at 10).
`let y: A.X = B()` works with a non-generic conformance (t5), so projection at name resolution is fine.
The goal printed is ((A::P).X ~ B) and it is not reduced to B ~ B; the second requirement does not use the witness found for P<A>.

No existing routine normalizes projections after instantiation: dealiased handles only TypeAlias, and reify only beta-reduces UniversalType applications. typeOfImplementation and aliasesInConformance fire only during member name resolution.

verdict.reasoning:
I re-ran every major claim on both frozen binaries, with at most 2 processes and timeout 300, and read the cited code.

Symptom: holds. min.hylo is rejected. At cap 5 with no flags on impl10 it takes 7094 user matches, and with fixsubst alone at cap 10 it runs out of memory, as the reviewers reported. The trace shows P<A> resolved to `$<ConformanceDeclaration at min:4.1>`, and the next goal is still `((A::P).X ~ B)`.

Cause: mislabelled and too narrow.
(a) The qualification is not abstract. The trace of min.hylo shows `resolve P<T>: penalty 0: $i`, a reference to the callee's where-clause using. `$<abstract given>` is printed only for Self goals. typeOfImplementation (Typer.swift 3341-3364) builds an opaque AssociatedType whenever the witness is not a ConformanceDeclaration. `TypeStore.unifiable(AssociatedType, AssociatedType)` (TypeStore.swift 1165) unifies two projections only when one qualification is `.abstract`, so such a reference unifies with nothing else.
(b) No equality requirement is needed. v3 (T.X as a parameter type) and v7 (T.X as a return type) fail on both binaries. t12 also fails on both: a generic caller passes `y: U.X` to `h<U>(x: T.X)` and gets "cannot pass value of type '(U::P).X' to parameter '(U::P).X'". So the defect is how a signature that mentions a projection is instantiated, not how a requirement is discharged.
(c) "eqrefute does not apply" is false. With eqrefute, and with fixsubst,eqrefute, at cap 10: eqrefute.refuted=2, 292 matches, about 30 ms, a clean error. eqrefute refutes a true equality.
(d) The generic-caller case regresses. The baseline accepts v5 (0 diagnostics, 92k matches, 1.7 s), and its trace runs through symmetry and transitivity with unbound middle variables (%dj4). This is the bug #1 path, and `$y` with the same printed type fails to match the goal directly. Under fixsubst,eqrefute it is rejected in 36 ms. This matters for Recommendation 2.
(e) Reflexivity v6 is accepted (0 diagnostics), so "never discharged" is overstated, though only slightly.

Fix: right in spirit, since it uses the found witness. As written it is insufficient:
- "Substitute into later requirements" misses the head (v3 and v7 have no later requirement).
- "Concrete qualifications" misses generic callers (t12, v5).
- `introduce(types:usings:)` (Typer.swift 1904) keeps only the declared types of the usings, so nothing yet maps a using declaration to its premise position.
- Premises are discharged last-first: the t4 trace shows `$1` proven while `$0` is still pending.
- Normalization must run before equalityIsRefuted, or eqrefute keeps rejecting.

Rejected or downgraded:
- The generic/conditional-conformance issue. Its evidence (t13) does not isolate the cause. My j1 uses a non-generic `given Box<B> is P` and gets the same "expression does not denote a type", so the failure is in resolving `Box<B>.X` as a type expression, not in instantiating a witness. The code-reading part is plausible but was not observed: declaredType(of: implementation) does not apply the witness's type arguments. I kept it only as a caveat.
- The coherence concern. Nothing was observed, so it stays info.
- The swapped where-clause order. It is a separate declaration-site scoping limitation and is not part of §3.

Also outside this section: table row 3 ("with concrete `T`") and Recommendation 3 should be reworded to match. The eqrefute/fixsubst recommendation should note the v5 regression.
